context.text: By 1453 the Roman Empire of the East was a city-state: Constantinople, a few Aegean islands, and the Morea, surrounded on every side by the Ottoman state. The union with Rome proclaimed at Ferrara–Florence in 1439, accepted by the emperor in hope of Western military aid, rejected by most of his people, had embittered the capital without saving it. In Hagia Sophia the union had been formally proclaimed only in December 1452, to widespread grief.

narrative.text: Sultan Mehmed II, twenty-one years old, invested the city in early April 1453 with an army modern estimates put at some 80,000 men and a train of great bombards; the defenders, Greeks and their Italian allies under the emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos and the Genoese commander Giustiniani, numbered perhaps 7,000. For seven weeks the Theodosian walls, which had turned back every besieger for a thousand years, held against the heaviest artillery yet assembled.

In the small hours of Tuesday, May 29, 1453, Mehmed launched his general assault. Giustiniani was wounded and carried off; the Janissaries forced the stockade at the breached Mesoteichion; and the last emperor, refusing flight, died fighting at the walls, his body was never certainly identified. By morning the City had fallen. The great church of Hagia Sophia, where the people had gathered for a final Liturgy through the night, was converted to a mosque within days.

Mehmed shortly reconstituted the Ecumenical Patriarchate, installing the anti-unionist monk Gennadius Scholarius as patriarch in 1454 and making him civil head (ethnarch) of the empire's Orthodox Christians, the beginning of the millet system under which the Church would live for four centuries.

significance.text: May 29, 1453 ends the eleven-century history of the Christian Roman Empire and begins the Ottoman captivity of the Greek Church, an age of survival, compromise, and new martyrs. In Orthodox memory the fall is mourned without despair: the empire passed, the Church did not. Leadership within the Orthodox world began shifting north, and within a century and a half Moscow had been raised to a patriarchate, articulating its self-understanding as the 'Third Rome.'

consequences.text: The patriarchate under Ottoman rule preserved the faith at heavy cost; Greek scholars carried manuscripts west, feeding the Renaissance; and the center of gravity of Orthodox political life moved to the rising Muscovite state.
